subject: Choosing range and variance priors for SPDE

messages.author: 03bc4090a2c2b3fb
messages.subject: Choosing range and variance priors for SPDE
parts:
Hello INLA team,

I am attempting to do a sensitivity analysis on priors for an SPDE model, but I'm having trouble interpreting the posterior hyperparameters from a model using default priors (i.e., inla.spde2.matern() ). I'm also unsure how to choose range and variance parameters to use in inla.spde2.pcmatern(). What would constitute a non-informative prior?

Thank you!
Pascale

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Choosing range and variance priors for SPDE
parts:
Hi Pascale,

The default priors in inla.spde2.matern are just that; "default". They only exist to make it easy to run simple tests. Any actual data analysis should set the priors to more sensible values for the problem at hand. The 2015 Lindgren&Rue JSS paper presented one way of doing that, but for all new analysis (with the exception of some nonstationary models) I strongly recommend using inla.spde2.pcmatern() instead, since
the pc-priors tend to be much nicer to work with. Check the Fuglstad et al paper on pc-priors for matern models for more information. The help text for inla.spde2.pcmatern has the reference, and also text about the priors

Practically speaking, there isn't really such a thing as non-informative priors (e.g. flat priors can be highly informative), but the pc-priors for spde model come close, in the sense that they don't impose strong constraints on the parameters, but at the same time tend to stabilise the inference. That said, it's still important to consider the prior parameter settings in the context of the problem.
For example, reasonable values for sigma tend to be very different for "additive Gaussian noise" observations, than for fields in log-linear predictors, since the standard deviation on the log-scale has such an important effect on the nonlinear predictor variability.

Finn
